item.title: Ice-dynamic regime of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream derived from the mass flux balance of englacial units
item.dc:creator: Charlotte Carter, Steven Franke, Daniela Jansen, Niklas Neckel, Olaf Eisen
item.description:
Annals of Glaciology — matched: ice sheet, ice stream, subglacial, ice flow, englacial, Greenland, Northeast Greenland Ice Stream
An assumption commonly used for ice streams in ice sheet models is that the vertical profile of horizontal velocity is constant throughout the ice column from the surface to the base.Here, we use airborne radar data for mass flux balance analysis of the central part of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream, to ascertain whether this assumption is broadly applicable in the ice stream's central region where the ice flow appears to be channelled by a large subglacial trough.We investigate the along-flow evolution of mass flux balance of both the full ice thickness and three englacial units in steady-state, and analyse the spatial variation of their imbalances.We assess the potential over-and under-estimation of ice flow velocity within the ice column and infer vertical shear profile models for our study region.These inferences suggest that the ice stream in this central region is flowing as a block, or plugflow, rather than with deformation from internal shearing, despite large variations in bed topography, basal shear stresses, and in a region with relatively slow ice flow velocities.

item.title: Ice surface change drives subglacial hydrologic reorganization and interior speedup in northwest Greenland
item.dc:creator: Aleah Nicholson Sommers, Aaron Stubblefield, Lauren C. Andrews, Colin Meyer, Benjamin Smith
item.description:
Journal of Glaciology — matched: ice sheet, subglacial, subglacial hydrology, ice dynamics, Greenland, basal melt, mass loss
Abstract Changes in ice surface elevation and slope influence subglacial water pressure and sliding velocity. Leveraging changes in elevation observed by the Ice, Cloud and land-Elevation satellite (ICESat) and ICESat-2 missions, we use coupled subglacial hydrology–ice dynamics modeling applied to a section of the northwest Greenland ice sheet to explore (i) how decadal-scale changes in ice surface elevation influence changes in winter background subglacial hydrology and corresponding ice velocity, and (ii) how much seasonal response is attributable to geometry versus environmental forcing. Our simulations suggest complex reorganization of the subglacial hydrologic system between 2004 and 2020, resulting from changes in surface elevation, driving redistribution of freshwater flux, an overall acceleration trend in the interior and an increase in background basal melt. Without changing hydrological conditions, geometry changes alone lead to greater interior acceleration, suggesting that changes in the subglacial system help to mitigate this speedup. We also find that the winter background state of the subglacial system modulates the seasonal response. This work demonstrates feedbacks that influence mass loss from the Greenland ice sheet as surface elevation evolves, highlighting the subtleties involved in accounting for changes in effective pressure, ice velocity and basal melt due to changes in subglacial hydrology.

item.title: Landscape evolution at an emerging englacial esker in Southeast Iceland over weekly-to-annual timescales
item.dc:creator: K. A. Bennett, Amy Lally, Alicia M. Rutledge, Ari Koeppel, Christopher Scott Edwards, Lauren Edgar, … (+5)
item.description:
Journal of Glaciology — matched: ice sheet, ice-sheet modelling, englacial, glacier, ice core
Abstract Eskers are used to characterize glacial drainage systems to inform ice-sheet modeling. However, the connection between eskers preserved in the paleoglaciologic record and the conditions required to deposit them is not well understood, particularly for englacial eskers. We use uncrewed aerial vehicle data over weekly-to-annual timescales from 2021 to 2024 at Breiðamerkurjökull in Iceland to investigate how englacial eskers evolve after emerging from the glacier. During the study period, an esker emerged from an englacial conduit, experienced significant modification and was emplaced on the outwash plain at the edge of a proglacial lake. We find that englacial eskers experience significant erosion and modification as they interact with proglacial lakes or streams and their ice cores melt, implying that englacial eskers are not generally well preserved in the paleoglaciologic record. Both esker morphology and stratigraphy evolved over the study period, indicating that when observed in preserved englacial eskers, they do not necessarily reflect conduit emplacement conditions. Englacial eskers deposited at the edge of overdeepenings may be more likely to be preserved than those deposited elsewhere. Additionally, surface ice topography evolution is assessed to identify structural hazards at an esker-forming glacier margin, which is critical as glacial-related hazards increase in a warming climate.

item.title: Evidence for subglacial flooding in labyrinthine channels on Devon Island, Nunavut, Canada
item.dc:creator: Simona F. Ruso, Gordon R. Osinski, Anna Grau Galofre, Antero Kukko
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, subglacial, meltwater
We describe the morphological characteristics of anastomosing (labyrinthine) bedrock channels to enhance the current understanding of subglacial meltwater dynamics of the Innuitian Ice Sheet. Our work reveals a morphological similarity between labyrinthine channels and other landscapes modified by glacial floods. We argue that the presence of anastomosis, distinct erosional surfaces, and longitudinal profile slope breaks imply formation by short-lived episodes of erosion associated with floods.

item.title: Development of a semi-persistent floating terminus at San Quintín Glacier (Northern Patagonia Icefield), the last piedmont glacier in the Andes
item.dc:creator: Michał Pętlicki, Andrés Rivera, Jonathan Oberreuter, Jose Andres Uribe, Johannes Reinthaler, Francisca Bown
item.description:
Annals of Glaciology — matched: grounding line, glacier, calving, outlet glacier
Abstract The piedmont lobe of San Quintín Glacier, the largest outlet of the Northern Patagonia Icefield, has recently entered a phase of rapid frontal retreat. We present results from a helicopter-borne ground-penetrating radar (GPR) survey conducted in May 2019 in the terminal zone of the glacier, combined with satellite-derived ice velocity, frontal position and surface elevation change data. GPR measurements along the flowline indicate ice thicknesses of 215–240 m in the lowermost 1400 m of the glacier. The inferred grounding line is located approximately 1500 m upstream from the 2019 calving front. Analysis of surface elevation change in 2017–19 shows mean thinning rates of -5.43 plus or minus $\pm$ ± 1.58 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 upstream and -1.08 plus or minus $\pm$ ± 1.39 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 near the terminus. Satellite-derived velocities reach up to 1050 m a minus 1 $^{-1}$ − 1 in the lower glacier, with higher values observed in the later part of the observation period. Residual bed reflection power derived from the GPR profiles indicates the presence of water at the glacier bed in the terminal zone. Taken together, these observations are consistent with the development of a semi-persistent floating terminus, where basal water and buoyancy modulate surface elevation change and control frontal stability and calving style. The results provide new observational constraints on the transient behaviour of floating termini at fast-flowing outlet glaciers in lacustrine settings.

item.title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
item.dc:creator: Kate Duffy, Elise Penn, Tristan Ballard, August Posch, Thomas J. Vandal
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: data assimilation, reanalysis, ensemble, machine learning
arXiv:2611.18393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

item.dc:creator: Lingfei Zhang, Xiaowei Wang, Yazhen Jiang, Shuqing Wang, Menglin Si, Cheng Huang
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: Earth system model, Earth system
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) We developed a daily global dataset describing latent heat flux and the resistances that regulate land–atmosphere water and energy exchange from 2001 to 2020 at 0.05° resolution. The product was evaluated against 244 flux-tower sites and performs robustly across climates and ecosystems. It provides new information for studying drought, ecosystem water stress, land–atmosphere coupling, and Earth system models.

item.title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Ni\~{n}o Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
item.dc:creator: Bo Qin, Zeyun Yang, Qiaofei Xue, Yanan Ding, Jinyu Wang, Chaopeng Ji, … (+6)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: predictability, data assimilation
arXiv:2611.17854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The predictability of the El Ni\~{n}o-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Ni\~{n}o, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Ni\~{n}o development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

item.title: EGGS-WG: an open source global gridded stochastic weather generator derived from ERA5-Land
item.dc:creator: Alex Schuddeboom, Christian Zammit, David Plew, Piet Verburg, Aidin Jabbari
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
Stochastic Weather Generators are simple models that can be used to produce realistic, simulated weather. Specifically, they use a combination of statistical techniques and existing measurements to make possible futures. This paper documents the release and provides validation of an open-source modern model, EGGS-WG. It produces daily rainfall values and hourly air temperature and dew point temperature values. The simulation quality is shown to be high when validated against ERA5-Land.
